title: Newborn screening, infant feeding and safe sleep
blurb: Explain the newborn screening checks and their timing, support safe feeding, and give accurate safer sleep advice to reduce the risk of SIDS.
question: Jade's 3-week-old son settles better on his tummy, and she asks whether he can sleep that way. What should the nurse advise?

teach.body: The first weeks are when screening finds hidden conditions early and when good feeding and sleep habits begin. Formally, the NHS offers every baby a newborn and infant physical examination (NIPE), a newborn blood spot test and a newborn hearing screen; safer sleep advice aims to reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). Plain English: check the baby at set times, feed safely, and put the baby down on their back in a clear cot every time.
teach.cite: NIPE handbook (2025); NHS newborn blood spot test; Lullaby Trust

teach.caption: Parents can decline all or part of screening; the decision is recorded and the GP and health visitor are told.

head: Group
Conditions
rows: PKU, MCADD, MSUD, IVA, GA1, HCU, HT1
teach.caption: Parents can decline sickle cell, CF and hypothyroidism screening individually, but the metabolic diseases only as a group. SMA is tested in some areas only.

teach.h: Making up a formula feed safely
items: Use first infant formula; it is the only formula needed in the first year unless there is a medical need.
Boil fresh water and use it within 30 minutes, so it is at least 70°C.
Put the water in the bottle first, then add the powder.
Cool the feed and check the temperature before feeding.
Feed responsively (paced feeding); never prop the bottle.

teach.body: Breastfeeding should start as soon as possible after birth, ideally within an hour, and a feed should be observed within the first 24 hours. Breastfeeding also lowers the risk of SIDS. Breastfed babies need a daily vitamin D supplement of 8.5 to 10 micrograms from birth; formula-fed babies taking 500 mL or more a day do not, as formula is fortified.

letters.word: Keep baby in your room for 6 months

teach.h: When sharing a bed is very dangerous

rows.label: Anyone in the bed has drunk alcohol
Anyone smokes, or smoking in pregnancy
Born before 37 weeks or under 2.5 kg

teach.note: Falling asleep with a baby on a sofa or armchair greatly increases the risk of SIDS (Lullaby Trust). Advice applies to 12 months, adjusted for prematurity.

teach.text: A baby who 'settles better on his tummy' should still be put on his back for every sleep, day and night. Tummy time is for when the baby is awake and supervised. Rolled towels, wedges and positioners do not make side or front sleeping safe.

teach.h: Scenario: Theo, 6 weeks, at a home visit
teach.body: On a home visit to 6-week-old Theo, community children's nurse Maya notices the nursery thermometer reads 24°C, and Theo is asleep under a thick quilt with a pillow. She explains that the room should be 16 to 20°C, removes the pillow and quilt, and shows his parents how to use a baby sleeping bag or a firmly tucked blanket with his feet at the foot of the cot. She checks he sleeps on his back in their room.

items: NIPE within 72 hours and again at 6–8 weeks.
Blood spot on day 5 for 10 conditions; results usually by 6 weeks.
Formula: water at least 70°C, used within 30 minutes, water before powder.
On the back, every sleep, in a clear flat cot, room 16–20°C, in parents' room for 6 months.
No sofa or armchair sleeping with a baby; bed sharing very dangerous after alcohol, smoking or sedatives.

summary: You can now explain when and why each newborn screen happens and what an abnormal finding means. You can also support safe breastfeeding and formula feeding and give accurate safer sleep advice.

A.q: Jade's 3-week-old son settles better on his tummy, and she asks whether he can sleep that way. What should the nurse advise?
options: Tummy sleeping is fine if he settles
Side sleeping with a rolled towel
On his back for every sleep
Tummy for naps, back at night
A.why: Safer sleep advice is to place the baby on their back for every sleep, day or night.

whyNot.0: Front sleeping increases the risk of SIDS, however well the baby settles.
whyNot.1: Side sleeping is not a safe position, and rolled towels add risk.
whyNot.3: The back position applies to daytime naps as well as night sleep.

A.q: Baby Oscar was born on Monday morning. His mother asks when his blood spot test will be done. What should the nurse say?
A.why: The blood spot test is usually done on day 5, counting the day of birth as day 0: Saturday for a Monday birth.

whyNot.0: 48 hours is too early for the routine test.
whyNot.2: Testing at discharge on day 0 is too early for reliable results.
whyNot.3: The 6–8 week check is the second NIPE examination, not the blood spot test.

A.q: Lucy is making up formula. She puts powder in the bottle, then adds water from a kettle boiled 2 hours ago. What should the nurse advise?
options: Use cooled boiled water from the fridge
Use warm tap water and shake well
Use bottled mineral water at room temperature
Add powder after water boiled within 30 minutes
A.why: NHS advice: use water at least 70°C (boiled no more than 30 minutes earlier), and put the water in the bottle before the powder.

whyNot.0: Cold water does not reach the 70°C needed to kill bacteria in the powder.
whyNot.1: Warm tap water is well below the 70°C needed.
whyNot.2: Room temperature water does not reach 70°C.

B.q: Baby Ellie is 30 hours old. Her mother asks what the newborn physical examination checks. Which areas does NIPE focus on?
B.why: The NIPE screening examination focuses on the eyes, heart, hips and, in boys, the testes.

whyNot.1: Hearing is a separate screen, and reflexes and skin are not the NIPE screening focus.
whyNot.2: Growth measurements are part of routine care, not the four NIPE screening areas.
whyNot.3: These are not the NIPE screening elements; blood conditions are found by the blood spot test.

B.q: During Ahmed's NIPE examination the red reflex is abnormal in one eye. What is the expected referral?
B.why: NIPE: an abnormal red reflex needs assessment by an ophthalmologist within 2 weeks.

whyNot.0: Waiting to 6–8 weeks is too long for an abnormal red reflex.
whyNot.2: A 12-month recheck would delay diagnosis of conditions such as cataract.
whyNot.3: Childhood vision screening does not replace urgent specialist review.

B.q: Priya's 10-week-old daughter sleeps in a cot beside her bed. Friends say she can move her into her own room now. What is the best advice?
options: Room share for at least 6 months
Move her at 3 months if feeding well
Move her once she sleeps through
Room share for the first 4 weeks
B.why: Safer sleep advice is to room share for at least the first 6 months.

whyNot.1: Three months is earlier than the recommended 6 months.
whyNot.2: Sleeping through is not the basis of the advice; age is.
whyNot.3: Four weeks is far shorter than the recommended 6 months.

C.q: A health visitor reviews four sleeping situations described by parents of young babies. Which carries the highest risk of SIDS?
options: Baby on back in a cot in the parents' room
Baby in a sleeping bag in a room at 18°C
Baby on back in a Moses basket by the bed
Parent falls asleep with baby on a sofa
C.why: Falling asleep with a baby on a sofa or armchair greatly increases the risk of SIDS.

whyNot.0: On the back in a cot in the parents' room is the safest arrangement.
whyNot.1: A sleeping bag in a room at 16–20°C follows safer sleep advice.
whyNot.2: A Moses basket beside the bed is a recommended own sleep space.

C.q: Baby Ada is 5 weeks old. Her parents declined cystic fibrosis screening but accepted the rest of the blood spot test. They now want CF screening after all. What is correct?
options: No, CF screening ends at 4 weeks
Yes, as she is under 8 weeks
No, a decline cannot be reversed
No, it waits for the 6–8 week NIPE
C.why: Babies are eligible for blood spot screening up to 1 year, except for CF, which is unreliable after 8 weeks. At 5 weeks Ada can still be screened.

whyNot.0: CF screening remains reliable up to 8 weeks, not 4.
whyNot.2: Babies remain eligible for screening, so parents can still accept it within the reliable window.
whyNot.3: The NIPE examination does not include CF screening.

C.q: Sam smokes and his partner had two glasses of wine tonight. Their baby, born at 36 weeks, is 3 weeks old. They ask about bringing her into their bed. What is the best advice?
options: Bed sharing is safe if she is between them
Use a pillow to keep her in position
Sleep with her on the sofa tonight instead
Put her in her own cot beside the bed
C.why: Bed sharing is very dangerous when a parent smokes or has drunk alcohol, or the baby was premature. The safest place is her own clear cot or Moses basket beside the bed.

whyNot.0: Lying between adults does not remove the risks from smoking, alcohol and prematurity.
whyNot.2: Sleeping with a baby on a sofa is even more dangerous.

reteach.title: Check, feed, back
reteach.question: What three messages should every new parent leave with?

blocks.body: Screen: NIPE within 72 hours and at 6–8 weeks, blood spot on day 5, hearing in the first weeks. Feed: breastfeed early and often, or make formula with water at least 70°C. Sleep: back, clear flat cot, 16–20°C, in the parents' room for 6 months, never asleep with the baby on a sofa.

blocks.text: The 6–8 week check is a second NIPE examination, not the blood spot test. The blood spot is done on day 5.

explain.body: A full physical examination focusing on eyes (red reflex), heart, hips and testes, done within 72 hours and again at 6–8 weeks, usually in primary care for the second check. Pulse oximetry is not a universal screen.

test.q: During the newborn examination of Jacob, neither testis can be felt. What is the expected action?
test.why: NIPE: impalpable testes (or hypospadias) need urgent senior review within 24 hours.

whyNot.0: GP review at 6–8 weeks is for a palpable undescended testis without hypospadias.
whyNot.1: Waiting 12 months delays assessment of possible serious causes.
whyNot.3: Ultrasound at 4–6 weeks is the hip screening pathway.

explain.body: Heel prick on day 5 (day 0 = birth) for 10 conditions. Results usually arrive by 6 weeks. Eligible up to 1 year, except CF which is unreliable after 8 weeks.

test.q: Which condition is included in routine newborn blood spot screening in England?
test.why: Congenital hypothyroidism is one of the 10 blood spot conditions.

whyNot.1: Hips are checked by NIPE examination.
whyNot.2: Cataract is detected by the red reflex in NIPE.
whyNot.3: Hearing has its own newborn hearing screen.

explain.body: Breastfeed within the first hour if possible; breastfeeding lowers SIDS risk. Breastfed babies need vitamin D drops. Formula: first infant formula, water at least 70°C, water before powder, paced feeding.

test.q: Amara is exclusively breastfeeding her 2-week-old. She asks whether the baby needs any supplements. What is correct?
options: Vitamin D from 6 months of age
test.why: Breastfed babies are advised to have a daily vitamin D supplement of 8.5 to 10 micrograms from birth.

whyNot.0: Vitamin D for breastfed babies starts from birth, not 6 months.
whyNot.2: Vitamin D is advised from birth, not from weaning.
whyNot.3: Vitamin K is given at birth (IM), not as weekly drops.

explain.body: Back for every sleep, clear flat cot, room 16–20°C, room share for at least 6 months, feet to foot of the cot. Avoid sofa sleeping. Bed sharing is very dangerous after alcohol, smoking, sleepy medicines or drugs, or for babies born before 37 weeks or under 2.5 kg.

test.q: Which room temperature is recommended for a sleeping baby?
test.why: The Lullaby Trust recommends a room temperature of 16 to 20°C.

whyNot.1: 21–24°C risks overheating, a SIDS risk factor.
